author_paragraphs.paragraph: God, or the manufacturer, had created the speakers in stereo pairs for good measure, to *breed abundantly in the earth, and be fruitful, and multiply upon the earth*. Or at least some sonic version of it, meant to harmoniously fill a waiting world. But even Babel had one tower. Los Angeles had none, which presented a difficulty: there was no single humanity to dissolve into. It wasn't one city; it was Southern California, a sprawl of parcels some lonely engineers had stitched together with freeways. That became evident the moment my car radio started announcing the weather in the form of roads and intersections, and of neighborhoods with names, none of which was Los Angeles. The freeways carried their own accents and dialects, and a strange notion of who belonged where. I would become a voice in it, eventually, but only in pieces: a part in this parcel, a part in that one.

The first nights were loud from above. LAPD helicopters circled low, searchlights sweeping the streets and loudspeakers addressing people below, as though someone up there were trying to arrest the whole neighborhood at once. In full honesty, I neglected to check the morning paper in case a string of alien abductions had afflicted the town. But that would at least have settled a question I'd brought with me from Madison, about how a place this big and this unruly could possibly be governed. Los Angeles, it seemed, had simply outsourced the job to some sort of aliens.

I had been there only a few weeks when we heard the shots. My roommate confidently claimed they were fireworks from a religious festival that fell on that very day. If that's how religion sounded here, then I thanked the heavens (or whatever it was that had been peering down from them lately) for my own apostasy. Being a skeptic also helped: I believed him for about as long as it took the sirens to arrive. You don't approach a bear while she's still angry, especially if she's the golden California kind. Then I went out. Across the street, two people were lying on the sidewalk. One was already under a sheet. The other was getting the kind of CPR you keep giving someone who has already passed.

When the brothers took up the annual question of who was most likely to become what, I ended up in a tie with myself: either I would move to Seattle and open a winery, or a brewery (there was some debate), or I would move to Seattle and eventually become the mayor of Redmond, Washington. This was based on solid evidence. It was widely known, and entirely true, that Sam had once decided he felt like going to Seattle, got in his car, drove there for no reason, turned around and drove all the way back. It was also known that when Hermosa Beach grew tiresome, I would drive to San Diego just to jog along its lagoon, because I could. The brothers were better forecasters than they knew. I did move to Seattle eventually, and did, in a manner of speaking, become an economy. But before any winery or mayoralty could materialize, a later chapter of my life intervened, and the brothers' prophecy remains, like most prophecy six-packs, two-thirds fulfilled.

Before leaving, Peter had written a note on his whiteboard: WE WANT JUSTICE. In his original context, "justice" meant *please don't drink my cognac*. We interpreted it as a call for spiritual reform. Sometime in that philosophical fog, we began chanting it back and forth down the empty hallway, "We want justice!", not protesting, not rioting, just cheerfully reciting Peter's whiteboard. Spirits (his) had created spirits (ours).

What we didn't know was that we weren't alone. The next morning, I learned that a third person had been in the house all night, in one of the few rooms downstairs, which we'd assumed were emptied. He had spent the night hunkered down, holding his breath, convinced from our chanting that the rioters had breached the upstairs of the house.

The next day, the riot had turned from the headline into a reality for us. The air smelled of burning and of that thoroughbred anger that takes decades to accumulate. In the morning, as the previous night's spirit settled, the thought struck me that if I had to escape the city for any reason, I had better have gas in my car. I drove out looking for a station that hadn't shut down, through streets lined with smoke and boarded windows, past familiar storefronts that were simply gone: the place I bought my fraternity cap, the restaurant my professor loved. At one station, I saw people streaming out of the convenience store. Excited, I pulled in for fuel, but pulled out just as quickly, like a man dodging alimony, when I realized those were looters. The gas station wasn't open; it had been opened.

That evening I moved to the greater safety inside the campus walls, taking refuge in a residence hall. From its upper floors I had a bird's-eye view of the surrounding city I had actually been inside earlier that day. It was like a movie, like nothing I had seen in real life: a full panorama of large pockets of fire as far as the eye could see, with the campus at its center, or at least like home plate, with everything laid out in front of it on all sides.

closing_paragraphs: A little over a week later, I did attend my commencement, the one I'd promised myself. It was a subdued ceremony, held on a campus surrounded by the city's fresh ruins, and the riots dominated the opening of the speeches. We had gathered to celebrate what we'd learned, and the city had just taught us what we hadn't.[^v1-c5-commencement]

When the smoke had thinned to a gray haze, I found myself split between the social jungle of Los Angeles and the industrial jungle to the north. In time, I would pack the Corolla for that northward drive. But before I left, I had already met a different kind of network in Los Angeles: a city of its own, made not of people but of machines, with its own rules for agreeing, its own failures to communicate, and, as it turned out, its own versions of the questions this chapter had been asking.
